Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room
Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: Threat items imply an ongoing personal-danger/being-followed formulation, which is hard to reconcile with trauma to a loved one; they read more like direct interpersonal victimization than fear for a loved one.

Within Threat, 'Checking Behind' and 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' reflect hypervigilant danger avoidance, while 'Risky Behavior' points in the opposite direction behaviorally; this combination is possible but clinically strained without any other items supporting disinhibition.

Memory item 'Pain Recall' implies bodily re-experiencing of injury to the patient's own body, which is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one unless she was also directly harmed; the other memory items do not suggest that.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, a prominent risky-behavior item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by fear/avoidance and reliving rather than self-endangering behavior. It pulls the threat profile in a different direction without support from other nodes.

issues.item: Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall in the same body parts as during the event implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma. That is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one, especially given no other items indicate direct physical victimization.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: The body-focused negative appraisals suggest distrust of one's own injured or trauma-reactive body, which fits direct bodily trauma better than trauma centered on harm to a loved one. In this profile they are not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, 'military topics' is hard to justify unless the loved one’s trauma was specifically military-related; that context is not represented anywhere else in the profile, so this trigger appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room
issues.explanation: 'Locked spaces' suggests a confinement/entrapment trauma context, but the rest of the profile centers on reliving, terror, and generalized danger after trauma to a loved one rather than a personal entrapment event. Without corroborating memory or appraisal content, this trigger looks clinically out of place.

vignette: At sixty-three, Rania had spent her adult life as a solitary auditor, but a single afternoon in a desert canyon had permanently fractured her sense of security. Three years ago, while hiking with her younger brother, a sudden monsoon had swollen a dry wash into a violent current. They had scrambled into a ranger’s maintenance shed, but the heavy steel door had slammed shut and the rusted latch had fused. In that locked space, the water rose, the temperature plummeted, and the natural world outside became a relentless, inescapable pressure against the walls. When they finally forced the door with a rock, her brother was already gone. The trauma had not been in the open trail, but in that confined darkness where nature offered no exit and the victim’s face had been the last thing she saw. This exact confluence of trapped confinement and wild terrain made the landscape itself a direct conduit to the event, ensuring that any similar setting would immediately bridge past and present. When the original triggers surfaced, they directly summoned the full sensory reliving of the canyon, flooding her with the exact terror she felt at the time. She would describe the flashbacks by saying the water and darkness filled her mouth and lungs exactly as they had that night, proving to her that her body was an enemy reacting to phantom danger. These intrusive memories immediately amplified her sense of threat, pushing her to avoid going to unfamiliar places because she could no longer assess the danger. Her conviction that she was powerless to stop bad things from happening, alongside her belief that her body was betraying her, directly fed the flashbacks; when she felt helpless, her mind would seize upon the locked-room memory to prove the world was inherently unsafe. Her loss of faith also made the original triggers feel more potent, as she could no longer dismiss the canyon or the locked cabin as mere history. The sheer weight of those confined rooms and wild terrain convinced her she had lost faith in life and higher powers, cementing her conviction that tragedy was inevitable. The chronic sleep deprivation and hypervigilance she maintained at work eroded her remaining trust in her own mind, solidifying her helplessness and loss of faith. The constant state of alarm made the original triggers feel overwhelmingly intrusive, forcing her to retreat from any setting that resembled a locked space or natural environment. Occasionally, the memory itself would spark a faint urge to check her surroundings, though that was a fleeting slip. The cycle tightened over the last eighteen months until her daily life narrowed to familiar perimeters. During a routine audit at a remote municipal building, she found herself unable to navigate the unfamiliar corridors, which forced her to request a permanent desk assignment in the familiar headquarters. This occupational limitation cemented her belief that she was fundamentally unsafe, which directly drove her threat responses, keeping her hypervigilant and unable to sleep even in her quiet apartment. When a locked elevator caught her between floors during an inspection, the full sensory reliving of the flood overwhelmed her completely, triggering the panic attacks that finally broke her routine. She realized she could no longer outrun the episodes, nor could she trust her own nervous system to distinguish past from present. The terror on recall and the triggered without warning symptoms bled into her daily routine, ensuring that every unfamiliar place felt like a tomb. Her helplessness and loss of faith solidified her avoidance of new environments, while her hypervigilance and sleep problems confirmed her worst fears about her body, creating a loop that felt both inescapable and logical. The original triggers continued to feed her negative beliefs, while her negative appraisals kept her hyperaware of every potential danger, ensuring that the memory would always return with full sensory intensity. Rania finally walked into the clinic because her close colleague had quietly arranged her leave, telling her she was disappearing, and because the sheer exhaustion of maintaining two lives was tearing her apart. She was most afraid that she would never feel safe in her own skin again, but what she hoped for, more than anything, was to wake up without bracing for a door that would never open.
